candidates.label: Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif
candidates.support: Wikidata's point for the Temple Mount is corroborated by scholarly archaeological reconstruction of the platform published by Ritmeyer; as a roughly 15-hectare platform, any single point is a center reference rather than a precise boundary.

summary.text: The Temple Mount is the raised platform in Jerusalem's Old City that Herod the Great enlarged to carry his rebuilt Second Temple, the center of Jewish worship in the first century AD. Herod began the work around 20-19 BC. The Jewish historian Josephus says the priests built the temple building itself in a year and six months, and that Herod built the cloisters and outer courts in eight years; but work went on for decades, and when the temple was finally finished, in the time of the governor Albinus, more than eighteen thousand workers were left without work. The cloisters of the outer court ran about six furlongs (roughly 1.1 km), including the Antonia fortress, which stood at the northwest corner and always held a Roman garrison. In John's Gospel, Jesus' hearers say the Temple "took forty-six years to build."

history.text: The Gospels describe Jesus visiting the Temple as a boy, found "sitting in the middle of the teachers," and later driving out those who sold oxen, sheep and doves there and overturning the money changers' tables. Acts describes Peter and John at the Temple, where a man lame from birth, laid daily at the gate called Beautiful, stood up and walked into the Temple with them, and later Paul being seized there by a crowd. These are only a sample: the word "temple" appears more than a hundred times in the New Testament.
Roman forces under the general Titus destroyed the Temple in AD 70. Its retaining walls, including the section known today as the Western Wall, survived as its most substantial remains.

Today the platform, also known as Haram al-Sharif, carries the Dome of the Rock, built in the seventh century, and the Al-Aqsa Mosque; these later buildings are outside this project's scope. Below the platform's western side, the Western Wall is a place of Jewish prayer.

scripture.textWEB: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions.
Jesus entered into the temple of God and drove out all of those who sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers’ tables and the seats of those who sold the doves.

They came to Jerusalem, and Jesus entered into the temple and began to throw out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers’ tables and the seats of those who sold the doves.
He found in the temple those who sold oxen, sheep, and doves, and the changers of money sitting.
Jesus went out from the temple, and was going on his way. His disciples came to him to show him the buildings of the temple.

A certain man who was lame from his mother’s womb was being carried, whom they laid daily at the door of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask gifts for the needy of those who entered into the temple.
Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive gifts for the needy.
Leaping up, he stood and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God.
When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the multitude and laid hands on him,
The Jews therefore said, “It took forty-six years to build this temple! Will you raise it up in three days?”

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch."

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Quirinius, governing Syria, conducted a census at the start of this period. Luke 2:1-2 is dated by some instead to the time of Herod's birth narrative, before 4 BC, rather than to Quirinius's AD 6 census; this note does not resolve the question.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod Agrippa I (ruler: Herod Agrippa I)
Roman province of Judea (ruler: Procurators, e.g. Antonius Felix, Porcius Festus)
Roman province of Judea (ruler: Legates, with a legion now based at Jerusalem)
politicalHistory.note: An administrative upgrade (a praetorian legate instead of a procurator), not a border or name change.
